The bus to Kharghar was so packed that Rukmini had to shout over the horns. "Aparna hardly talks, but her notebook is full of sketches. Faces, trees, even the canteen uncle."
Her cousin Nitin, squeezed against the door, yelled back a game. "Okay, which is more likely? One: Aparna is an artist. Two: Aparna is an artist, a shy one, and she secretly writes poems."
"Two! Obviously two," Rukmini said. "That's so her. I can totally see her writing poems at night."
Nitin grinned. "Every shy poet-artist is still an artist. So number two can't beat number one."
The bus braked hard and Rukmini grabbed the rail, frowning. "But two sounds more true."
"Sounds, yes," Nitin said. "You just added one more thing that has to be right."
Rukmini stayed quiet until her stop, still picturing Aparna's secret poems.

qa.a: It is full of sketches: faces, trees, even the canteen uncle.

qa.q: Why does option two feel more likely to Rukmini?
qa.a: The shy, poem-writing artist matches Rukmini's picture of Aparna so well that she can 'see' it, and that vivid fit feels truer than the plain option.

qa.q: What quick check could Rukmini use next time she compares two stories like this?
qa.a: She could ask whether one option is just the other one plus extra details; if it is, the shorter one is always at least as likely.

qa.q: How might Aparna feel if she knew her friends had turned her into a 'secret poet'?
qa.a: She might be amused, or a bit uneasy that people built a whole story about her from her quietness and her sketches.

Baljeet sat on the balcony of the family flat in Mohali, phone in hand, filling in the class magazine's "Where will we be in ten years?" poll. Each question had two choices. For Kiran, the quiet boy who spent every lunch break drawing in the corridor, the choices were: "Kiran will be an artist" or "Kiran will be a shy artist who also publishes poems."
Baljeet smiled and ticked the second one without a pause. It fit perfectly: the soft voice, the ink on his fingers, the way he stared out of windows.
Baljeet's older sister leaned over. "You think the longer one is likelier?"
"It's more him."
"But if he's the poem one, he's also the artist one. The first can't lose."
Baljeet looked at the screen again and felt a little silly, and a little stubborn. The second choice still felt right.

qa.a: Baljeet feels a little stubborn because the second choice matches everything Baljeet has noticed about Kiran, the soft voice, the ink, the staring out of windows. So the detailed picture feels truer even though it needs more things to be true.

I'm Wasim, and I still remember the museum trip in Class 9. Devika sat on the floor of the sculpture hall with her sketchbook while the rest of us took selfies. She hardly said a word all day.
On the bus back I told Farhan, "She's the shy type. Draws all day, writes poems at night. Definitely."
"Or she's just an artist," he said.
"No, poems. Look at her. It all fits." The more I added, the surer I felt. We bet a samosa.
Two weeks later, at the inter-school fair, Devika was running the art stall, loud and bossy, and when I asked about poems she laughed. "I hate writing. I only draw."
Farhan got his samosa. What bothered me later was that "artist" had always been the safer bet. Every extra detail I added was one more thing that had to be true.

Maths teacher's note, Class 9B, probability lesson (Mr Francis)
Today I put a question on the board: "A new student is quiet and draws in the margins of every notebook. Which is more likely? (a) The student is an artist. (b) The student is a shy, poem-writing artist."
Samir, 14, answered first and loudly: (b). "Because the quiet part explains the shy part, and artists who are shy usually write poems. It's a whole person, sir." About twenty hands went up with his.
I drew one big circle for "artists" and a smaller circle inside it for "shy, poem-writing artists". I asked Samir which circle a person could be in without being in the other. He stared at the board for a while and said, "The big one. Oh."
Next: tomorrow they will each write a story, then cross out one detail at a time and see how the chance changes.

qa.q: Which answer did Samir choose first?
qa.a: Samir answered (b), that the student is a shy artist who writes poems.

qa.q: Why did option (b) feel more likely to Samir?
qa.a: The extra details made a "whole person" that fit together, so it felt truer to Samir, even though it asked for more things to be true at once.

qa.q: What choice by Mr Francis helped Samir see the problem himself?
qa.a: Drawing a small circle inside a big one and asking which circle a person could be in alone let Samir discover the answer instead of being told.

qa.q: How might the twenty students who agreed with Samir feel after his "Oh"?
qa.a: Some may feel a bit embarrassed and others curious, realising they all fell for the same neat story, which may make them pay closer attention to the next lesson.

grounding: It shows a teenager judging a detailed description of a quiet student more likely than a simple one, though each detail makes it less probable.

passage:
Class 11 psychology, teacher's note, 14 November.
Today I gave the class a short story: "Meenal is quiet, wears paint-stained jeans, and spends breaks alone." Then two options. A: Meenal is an artist. B: Meenal is an artist who writes poetry and plans to live in a hill town. Keerthana, one of my sharpest students, picked B at once. "It just fits better," she said. Twenty-two of thirty-one students agreed with her.
I drew two circles on the board, "artists," and inside it a small one, "artists who write poetry and want hill towns." Keerthana stared. "B is inside A. It can't be more likely." She laughed, a little embarrassed.
Next class: I'll show them how adding details to rumours works the same way.

qa.q: How many of the thirty-one students agreed with Keerthana?
qa.a: Twenty-two of thirty-one students.

qa.q: Why did Keerthana laugh when she saw the circles?
qa.a: She felt a little embarrassed, seeing that the detailed option she found so fitting was inside the simpler one and couldn't be more likely.

qa.q: How did the teacher help the class, and why does the picture work?
qa.a: By drawing the small circle inside the big one, which shows that every extra detail makes a story narrower and less likely.

qa.q: How might Meenal, if she were real, feel about option B?
qa.a: She might feel boxed in by a detailed story that goes far beyond anything anyone knew about her.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a teenager choosing a detailed story as more likely than a simpler one, because details make it feel truer.
